subject: ventures/snow-removal-bid-calculator
professional: an owner-operator who bids residential and commercial snow plowing and salting contracts; they check first whether the per-push and seasonal for each customer come out in the local market band, whether a seasonal can be written the way contracts actually are (a visit cap or per-inch tiers with per-push overage beyond it), whether salt is priced the way they buy it (bags for walks, bulk tons for lots), and whether each stop on a mixed route gets its own price

evidence.correctness: node /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-oss-monorepo/c7bd76da-fba0-5582-91c4-a58d419f796f/scratchpad/snow/check.mjs /home/user/oss-monorepo/ventures/snow-removal-bid-calculator/calc.mjs recomputes by hand from the README's stated method (loaded = 22*1.3+45 = 73.60/h; push = ((plow+walk+deadhead)/60*73.6 + bags*8)*1.15; ice = (((plow+walk)*0.65+deadhead)/60*73.6 + 1.2*bags*8)*1.15; price = cost/0.8). Every figure matches to the cent: two-car 764.95, sidewalks 725.05, medium lot 2,871.96, two-car at 8/10/14 storms 663.99/764.95/966.86 (the vs-a-flat-seasonal-rate.html tables), 8-drive route 7,649.49, $2,800 proposal survives 1.78 storms. Against an outside source (bobvila.com snow-removal cost article, fetched): per visit $30-$95, seasonal $350-$450 'usually with limits on the total number of visits'; the tool's per-push for a single-car ($46.77) and two-car ($63.10) driveway sit inside the per-visit band. Held at 2: the 'Per-site seasonal' and 'Per-site per-push' outputs (index.html:197-198, calc.mjs:143-144) are the route total divided by the number of stops, so on a mixed route they are wrong for every stop: a two-car driveway plus a medium lot shows $2,273.07 per site where the driveway alone prices at $956.19 and the lot at $3,589.95. That is the flat-rate error the venture's own vs-a-flat-seasonal-rate page warns against, on a figure a contractor would quote from.

Seven seeded mutations via platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: 5 caught (ice-minute factor 0.65->0.6, overhead dropped from ice events, deadhead dropped from ice visits, per-site per-push from cost instead of price, ice cost dropped from break-even), 2 survived (per ice-event price divided by (1-m) replaced with markup (1+m), calc.mjs:140, a headline output nothing asserts; per-push belowBreakEven < -> <=, calc.mjs:180). evidence.craft: Read calc.mjs (224 lines, pure, one number() validator, explicit allowZero), index.html module script (~lines 290-520), share.mjs (allowlisted keys), proposal.mjs header. Output written with textContent; the one innerHTML list interpolates preset labels only (readSites sets name from SITE_PRESETS), so no injection path. Defects: proposal.mjs is a 400+ line engine copied verbatim from platform/proposal (its header says so) rather than imported; a blank plow/walk field silently becomes 0 (input '' -> seasonal 529.65 with no warning); breakEvenSnowEvents is computed twice (calc.mjs:164 and :173) with the same formula.
evidence.claims: Disclaimer, no-upload privacy and DNT/GPC opt-out present and match usage.mjs. vs-aspire.html checked against youraspire.com (fetched): Chesterfield, MO (footer '390 S Woods Mill Rd #300 Chesterfield, MO 63017'), founders Mark Tipton and Kevin Kehoe, 'In 2013 ... began building' (the same page's FAQ also says 'founded in 2014'), snow and ice management offered, ServiceTitan acquisition 2021 (Aspire about page and Wikipedia citing TechCrunch 2021-06-30), no price published: all backed. Not backed: 'plans tiered by a contractor's annual revenue' and 'its site describes plans as scaled to a contractor's annual revenue' (vs-aspire.html:51, :87) - the page itself admits the pricing page was not reached, youraspire.com/pricing returns 404 and the home page says only 'pricing for every stage of business growth'. vs-a-flat-seasonal-rate.html:76 and :108 call $22/hr a 'loaded operator' rate; $22 is the base wage (loaded operator is 28.60, operator+truck 73.60). how-much-to-charge.html:44 calls fourteen storms 'a realistic winter in many Northeast and Midwest metros with a 1-inch trigger' with no climatology source. The hero '$350 seasonal that looked fine at eight storms' is only half backed by the tool's own defaults: a two-car driveway costs $403.82 at 8 storms and no ice, so $350 already loses at eight; a single-car one keeps 14.5% at 8/0 and loses at 14/4 ($653.15).
evidence.fitness: Walked the owner-operator job: a route of 30 mixed driveways plus two small lots, each billed separately, bid in October. The tool prices the route correctly in aggregate but gives each customer the route average, so the operator must run each stop as its own one-row bid to get a quotable figure. A seasonal cannot be written with a visit cap and per-push overage, or with per-inch tiers (bobvila: seasonal 'usually' limits visits; per-inch tiers common), which is how residential seasonals are sold. Salt is bags only; a lot is bought and spread by the ton. The break-even storm count and ice-as-its-own-line are genuinely useful for the 'sharpen the seasonal' conversation.
evidence.domain: Compared against common practice (bobvila.com cost article, fetched; SIMA guidance from knowledge, sima.org resources 404). Right: route minutes at a loaded operator-plus-equipment hourly, deadhead amortised per stop, margin on price not markup, ice priced separately, multiple passes per long storm. Departures: per-site price is a flat average; no seasonal visit cap, per-inch tier or overage; salt multiplied by passes per event (passes=2 doubles salt per storm though lots are usually salted once at clean-up, calc.mjs:124-128); salt in 50-lb bag units only, no tons/acre for commercial; commercial lots typically bid per equipment-hour by machine class, which a single truck rate cannot represent (stated limitation).

verdict: The arithmetic is right: every figure I recomputed by hand from the stated method matches to the cent, including both comparison-page tables, and per-push prices for default driveways fall inside an outside source's $30-$95 per-visit band. The method (loaded operator-plus-truck hourly, deadhead, ice as its own event, margin on price, break-even storms) is one a snow contractor would recognise. It does not meet the bar. The per-site seasonal and per-push it shows are route averages, so on a mixed route each customer is quoted wrongly, the flat-rate failure its own comparison page criticises; seasonals cannot carry a visit cap or depth tiers, which is how they are usually written; the Aspire page asserts revenue-tiered pricing it admits it could not check; and two of seven seeded mutations, one on the per ice-event price, survive 95 passing tests. Correctness, verification, claims, fitness and domain are 2; completeness and craft 3.
